title: Week 8 Mastery Quiz — Rome and Han China

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a major political transformation in Rome?
choices: Republican institutions disappeared immediately when Rome expanded beyond Italy.
Roman citizenship never changed after the early republic.
Rome moved from republican government through civil conflict toward imperial rule while some earlier institutions and offices continued in altered forms.
The Roman Empire was governed through the same institutions as Han China.
questions.explanation: Roman political transformation involved major change alongside institutional continuity.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes Han imperial administration?
choices: It depended only on hereditary kings with no central officials.
It used the fully developed examination system of much later imperial China without modification.
It copied Roman provincial government.
It combined imperial officials, territorial administration, household registration, taxation, law, and local relationships to govern a large realm.
questions.explanation: Han administration combined central institutions with territorial and local mechanisms; later examination systems should not be projected backward unchanged.

questions.prompt: Why should historians be cautious about describing the Silk Roads as one road connecting Rome directly to Han China?
choices: The networks involved multiple routes, regions, and intermediaries, and goods could travel farther than individual merchants.
Long-distance exchange did not exist.
Only armies used overland routes.
Han China prohibited all foreign exchange.
questions.explanation: Silk Road exchange operated through interconnected networks and intermediaries.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest interpretation of Romanization?
choices: Roman culture completely replaced every local culture.
Roman language, law, institutions, and practices spread unevenly and were adapted within local contexts.
Every province adopted Roman practices at the same rate.
It refers only to Roman military conquest.
questions.explanation: Romanization is best treated as uneven interaction and local adaptation, not uniform cultural replacement.

questions.prompt: Which comparison of Roman citizenship and Han political membership is most defensible?
choices: They were identical legal systems.
Han subjects voted in Roman-style assemblies.
Roman citizenship was a changing legal status, while Han subjects were organized through different imperial, household, administrative, and social categories.
Neither empire distinguished among legal or social statuses.
questions.explanation: The two empires organized political and social membership through different categories and institutions.

questions.prompt: Which evidence best demonstrates that a central imperial policy reached local communities?
choices: A law issued in the capital by itself
A modern textbook summary
The size of the empire on a map
Local administrative records, inscriptions, artifacts, or correspondence showing implementation or response
questions.explanation: Local evidence can show how central policies were implemented, negotiated, or resisted.

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains the role of infrastructure in both empires?
choices: Infrastructure helped move officials, soldiers, information, taxes, and goods, but control and integration remained uneven.
Roads automatically produced complete political control.
Infrastructure was used only for trade.
Frontier regions had no effect on imperial government.
questions.explanation: Infrastructure enabled imperial movement and administration without guaranteeing uniform control.

questions.prompt: Why is “collapse” an insufficient explanation for the end of Han rule and western Roman imperial government?
choices: Neither experienced political fragmentation.
Political fragmentation resulted from interacting pressures and was accompanied by significant institutional and cultural continuities.
One single cause explains both cases.
Both empires ended in the same century.
questions.explanation: Multiple causes interacted, and many institutions and traditions persisted beyond political fragmentation.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Rome after the fifth century CE is most accurate?
choices: All Roman government and institutions disappeared everywhere in 476 CE.
Han officials took control of the eastern Mediterranean.
The western imperial government fragmented while the eastern Roman Empire continued for centuries.
Roman law immediately ceased to influence later societies.
questions.explanation: The eastern Roman Empire continued long after western imperial fragmentation.

questions.prompt: Which comparison best demonstrates continuity-and-change reasoning?
choices: Rome and Han were the same because both were empires.
Both empires weakened only because of invasions.
List rulers without explaining relationships among events.
Identify which institutions, identities, practices, and networks persisted, which transformed, and how interacting pressures altered political structures in each case.
questions.explanation: Continuity-and-change reasoning analyzes persistence and transformation rather than reducing history to similarity or a single cause.

shortResponse.prompt: Using at least three specific pieces of evidence from Rome and Han China and at least two source types, explain how large empires built durable institutions and why those institutions later weakened, fragmented, or changed. Identify at least one important continuity after political fragmentation.
shortResponse.exemplar: Full-credit work makes a defensible comparison, uses accurate evidence from both empires and at least two source types, explains interacting causes rather than a single-cause collapse, and identifies a meaningful institutional, cultural, legal, or infrastructural continuity.
